candidats.titre: Can Home Visits Re-Engage Chronically Absent Students? Evidence from the LEAP Program -- by Eric Brunner, Shangyue Jiang, Stephen Ross
candidats.resume: Beginning in the summer of 2021, the state of Connecticut launched the Learner Engagement and Attendance Program (LEAP) where home visits by school personnel were conducted with students identified as chronically absent from Connecticut’s 15 most disadvantaged school districts. Home visits were designed to connect students and their families directly with teachers to foster strong connections. We use student-level data from 2021–22 through 2023-24 to estimate event studies of the effect of LEAP on student attendance, chronic absenteeism, disciplinary incidents, and student achievement. Utilizing models that address selection into treatment timing over student observable and unobservable attributes, we find that students who received the LEAP intervention experienced approximately a 4 to 5 percentage point increase in attendance rates, a 13 to 15 percentage point decline in chronic absenteeism, and a 3 to 5 percentage point decline in the number of disciplinary incidents. Notably, initial event studies indicated increasing treatment effects over time, but after correcting for selection on unobservables treatment effects appeared constant over time. These effects were broad based, with similar impacts by gender, race and ethnicity, and free or reduced-price lunch status. These attendance and discipline results provide suggest that the LEAP intervention increased student noncognitive skills.

candidats.titre: Saving for the Machines -- by Jesús Fernández-Villaverde
candidats.resume: When machines can perform a growing share of tasks, growth depends on two margins: how the task structure affects the returns to accumulating machines, and how strongly capital accumulation responds to those returns. I argue that, in a standard task model, capital supply governs the size of the growth boom associated with automation, while the task structure sets the duration of this growth boom and the evolution of wages. I document how the same technology path that generates 11.7% annual growth when households choose their saving rate optimally delivers only 2.2% when the saving rate is fixed at the calibrated U.S. 2025 level of 23%. Therefore, slow growth might reflect too little capital accumulation instead of a technological bottleneck. Also, the saving rate rises mainly because automation raises the capital share, not because households become thriftier. Long yields price the growth boom: the ten-year real yield jumps from 5.1% to 13.6% on impact. In my benchmark calibration, hand-to-mouth households lose the equivalent of two-fifths to two-thirds of their consumption, while keeping them on trend temporarily costs at most a fifth of GDP.

candidats.titre: Public R&D and the Automation of Manufacturing: Evidence from the Space Race -- by Apoorva Babbar, Shawn Kantor, Alexander Whalley, Jingyuan Zeng
candidats.resume: This paper examines how public research and development shaped the direction of technological change during the Cold War–era Space Race and its consequences for US manufacturing. While prior research has documented the effects of public R&D on innovation and economic growth, less is known about whether mission-oriented public investment directed innovation toward automation and how this affected labor markets. We exploit variation in exposure to NASA's Space Race investments across industries and locations to estimate the effects of public R&D on innovation and manufacturing outcomes from 1947 to 1992. Combining newly developed measures of automation in full-text patent data with historical evidence on government involvement in patenting, we show that NASA-sponsored patents are systematically more automation-intensive than non-NASA patents within the same technological classes. Industries and locations more exposed to Space Race activity experienced persistent declines in labor share, consistent with the diffusion of labor-saving technologies developed for space applications. In contrast, we find little evidence of systematic changes in skill composition. These findings show that mission-oriented public R&D can shape the direction of technological change and have lasting distributional consequences.

candidats.titre: Aggregate-Surplus Maximizing Monetary Policy -- by David Baqaee, Ariel Burstein, Joao Guerreiro
candidats.resume: We study optimal monetary policy in a general heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian (HANK) economy. Instead of maximizing a social welfare function, the policymaker maximizes the joint surplus of all households, without taking a stance on how that surplus should be distributed. This is the policy that maximizes resources left over if winners from reform were to compensate losers. We derive the approximate optimal policy using linear-quadratic methods. The quadratic objective function nests the standard New Keynesian loss function and adds losses from incomplete markets and heterogeneous labor wedges. We show that optimal policy is the sum of time-dependent and state-contingent components. When labor wedges are homogeneous, monetary policy cannot improve household insurance: the time-dependent component is zero, and optimal policy coincides with the representative-agent New Keynesian (RANK) benchmark. Departures from RANK arise from heterogeneous labor wedges. In that case, the time-dependent component temporarily alleviates incomplete-market distortions but vanishes over time. The state-contingent component solves a dual-mandate problem, as in RANK, but with a higher weight on output-gap stabilization relative to inflation stabilization. In a calibrated model, heterogeneous labor wedges raise this weight by about 37 percent. We also find that a dual mandate with this higher weight achieves almost all of the aggregate-surplus gains from the full optimal policy and requires no compensatory transfers between winners and losers.

candidats.titre: The Effects of Monetary Policy on Macroeconomic Expectations: High-Frequency Evidence from Prediction Markets -- by Eric T. Swanson, Wang Renxuan, Yanbin Wu
candidats.resume: When the Federal Reserve raises interest rates, standard macroeconomic models and VARs predict that output, employment, and inflation should fall over the next several quarters. However, monthly-frequency professional macroeconomic forecast revisions are sometimes positively correlated with Fed interest rate changes, leading to a debate about what could explain these puzzling correlations. We bring to bear new high-frequency data on this question from macroeconomic event contracts traded on Kalshi, a CFTC-licensed, U.S.-based event trading exchange and prediction market. These high-frequency event contracts allow us to isolate and estimate the effects of monetary policy and other announcements on Kalshi market-implied macroeconomic expectations. Our results are consistent with standard transmission channels from monetary policy to the macroeconomy, with little or no role for a “Fed Information Effect”.

candidats.titre: Coase Meets Negishi: Property Rights, Welfare Weights, and Distributional Consequences in Climate Economics -- by Simon F. Lang, Matthew D. Gordon, Matthew J. Kotchen
candidats.resume: We develop a property-rights based approach for defining welfare weights in economic models of climate change. Whether there is a "right to pollute" or a "right to no pollution" is increasingly contested in legislatures, courts, and international climate negotiations. We show how these notions of property rights can provide the basis for "Coasean welfare weights" that are applicable in multilateral public goods settings. Distributional questions are addressed through positive analysis, conditional on property rights, rather than normative views about redistribution. The implied transfers are consistent with a bargained solution over the net benefits of addressing climate change and reflect the value of property rights over emissions. The approach defines efficient allocations that generate Pareto improvements, in contrast to commonly used Negishi weights. We implement the approach in a global integrated assessment model to quantify what countries have at stake in ongoing political and legal debates about emissions-related property rights.

candidats.titre: Governance Regimes, Economic Mobility, and the Composition of Public Investment: Evidence from the Democratization of Villages in India -- by Andrew D. Foster, Mark R. Rosenzweig
candidats.resume: We develop a quantifiable general-equilibrium model of village governance, motivated by India’s democratization, to study how political institutions shape public goods provision and economic development. The model features two groups, landowners and landless workers, with different preferences over public goods such as irrigation, schools, and employment programs. Households from both groups can enter nonfarm entrepreneurship, but face credit-dependent entry costs. We compare oligarchy, where landowners control public goods decisions, with democracy, where electoral competition determines policy based on the relative sizes of the two groups. The calibrated model predicts that democratization’s effects on public goods and growth are not uniform; they depend on population composition and the ease of occupational mobility through access to credit. Using a 37-year village-level panel from India (1971–2006) and exploiting variation in democratization driven by state and national reforms, we find strong support for these predictions. Financial intermediation shifts landless households’ preferences from wage-enhancing policies toward schooling, increasing nonfarm business entry. As a result, democracy provides fewer schools than oligarchy when credit is unavailable, but more schools when credit is accessible. We also show that transfers to the landless increase schooling under democracy but reduce it under oligarchy. These findings highlight how governance structures and economic conditions jointly determine the effectiveness of development policies.

candidats.resume: by Gina Polo Infante, Marino Mejía Rocha, Katerine Ariza Ruiz, Jeannette Liliana Amaya Lara, José Andrés Ocaña Navas, Andrés Peralta Chiriboga, Ana Sofía Zea Ruiz, Natalia Arcila Toro, Anita Gabriela Villacís, Gilma C. Mantilla C, Enrique Peñaloza Quintero, Ana Lucía Torres Castillo, Zulma M. Cucunubá, José Andrés Corredor Martínez, David Olaya Escobar, on behalf of LAC Hub for Climate Change and Health (CLIMAS) Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) is highly vulnerable to climate change despite contributing minimally to global greenhouse gas emissions. Climate-related hazards — including extreme heat, floods, droughts, and hurricanes — exacerbate health risks and disproportionately affect Indigenous peoples, Afro-descendant populations, rural communities, women, older adults, and individuals with chronic conditions. candidats.titre: La ménopause peut discrètement fragiliser les os, voici ce qu’il faut savoir pour les protéger
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL À la ménopause, les changements hormonaux peuvent mener à une perte de densité osseuse. Cette perte de densité osseuse, qui peut déboucher sur le développement d’une ostéoporose, commence parfois longtemps avant la fin des règles. La détecter tôt permet de mettre en place des mesures pour la freiner : modification de l’alimentation, activité physique, traitements médicamenteux… Les squelettes qui, à l’époque d’Halloween, se retrouvent suspendus aux portes des voisins ou mis en scène dans leurs jardins semblent être des structures immuables. Celui qui constitue notre charpente interne, cependant, ne cesse de se transformer. Aux alentours de la ménopause, ces modifications peuvent basculer vers une perte osseuse, le plus souvent sans qu’aucune douleur ni aucun autre symptôme ne se manifestent. En tant que chercheuse spécialiste de la biologie du squelette à la faculté de médecine de la Washington University de Saint-Louis, j’étudie la manière dont les signaux hormonaux et métaboliques influencent le renouvellement osseux. La ménopause est à mes yeux un moment privilégié pour aborder les questions touchant à la santé du squelette. La ménopause n’est confirmée qu’au terme de douze mois consécutifs sans survenue de règles , en l’absence de toute autre explication. Cependant, la perte osseuse qui peut résulter de ce changement peut commencer à s’accélérer dès avant la fin des règles. Autrement dit, la perte osseuse peut s’emballer avant même qu’une femme sache que ses dernières règles étaient bel et bien les dernières. Pourquoi l’os se modifie-t-il à la ménopause ?…

candidats.resume: Robin Williams , Monica Vitti , Patrick Stewart or French actress Nathalie Baye : all these famous people lost their lives to dementia with Lewy bodies . This neurocognitive disease is only tends to get publicity when a celebrity dies from it. Yet it is a common disease (and one of the most common forms of dementia) , in France alone it affects about 250,000 people, which makes it the country’s second most widespread neurodegenerative disease , after Alzheimer’s, putting on a par with Parkinson’s . It is estimated that dementia with Lewy bodies (commonly known as “DLB”) affects more than 10 million patients worldwide . What causes the disease? What symptoms should we look out for? How is it treated? Here is what you need to know. A long-ignored illness Dementia with Lewy bodies owes its name to inclusions that develop inside patients’ neurons called “ Lewy bodies ”, after the German-born doctor Friedrich Heinrich Lewy, who first discovered their existence in 1912. However, it was only in 1976 that the first clinical case was formally described, while the first international clinical criteria were defined much later in 1996. In its earliest stages (the prodromal stage before full-blown dementia develops , followed by the early, milder stage ), dementia with Lewy bodies is characterised by the dysfunction of certain parts of the outer layers of the brain, such as the insula and the olfactory bulbs (OB) . candidats.titre: Des mots qui effacent les animaux ? Ce que révèle l’écriture scientifique
candidats.resume: Les scientifiques emploient souvent, dans les publications où ils décrivent leurs expérimentations faites sur des animaux, des termes qui effacent les souffrances de ces derniers. Fourni par l'auteur L’ESSENTIEL Les formulations qu’utilisent les scientifiques dans les publications décrivant des expérimentations sur les animaux chosifient ces derniers et effacent souvent leur souffrance. Les terminologies que les scientifiques choisissent effacent également leur rôle, en disant, par exemple, « le sevrage a eu lieu » plutôt que « nous avons séparé les porcelets de leur mère ». Ces choix linguistiques orientent ensuite leurs façons de penser et d’agir. Imaginons l’expérience scientifique suivante : des canards sont suralimentés pendant plusieurs semaines afin de produire du foie gras. Des scientifiques réalisent des observations comportementales, puis des abattages et des pesées d’organes dans l’objectif de mesurer l’impact du gavage sur le comportement et l’état corporel des canards. Comment décrire ce que ces derniers vivent ? Doit-on écrire « l’intégrité corporelle des animaux a été évaluée » ou plutôt « les expérimentateurs ont quantifié les lésions sur le corps des canards » ? Cette différence de formulation en dit long sur la façon dont les scientifiques parlent de ce qu’elles ou ils font aux animaux ou, au contraire, sur la façon dont leurs actes sont passés sous silence. Car la manière dont les expérimentateurs et expérimentatrices mettent en mots leurs recherches n’est pas neutre. candidats.titre: Ce nouveau langage scientifique qui adoucit la destruction du vivant
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL La mode n’est pas qu’une question de vêtements ou de musique, elle touche aussi le langage scientifique. Certains mots sont sélectionnés, encouragés ou abandonnés par les scientifiques. Ceux utilisés pour décrire les causes et les conséquences de la destruction de la biodiversité ne font pas exception. Depuis une trentaine d’années, une série de mots colonisent ainsi le vocabulaire employé par les scientifiques en présentant la situation écologique sous un angle managérial. De quoi aligner les résultats de la science avec les exigences du capitalisme. Cherchez l’erreur dans ces deux formulations : « Notre ambition est de faire de l’alimentation une solution qui préserve et régénère la nature tout en renforçant la résilience des systèmes agricoles. » « Protéger une savane artificielle est une solution fondée sur la nature pour restaurer le carbone et la biodiversité. » Premier indice : ces deux formules sont pleines de promesses. « Régénérer la nature » ou « restaurer le carbone et la biodiversité » sonnent comme des petits miracles. Autre indice : les deux formules utilisent des termes un peu techniques et mystérieux, comme « résilience » et « solution fondée sur la nature », qui méritent une explication. Ces deux énoncés ont autre chose de commun : ils pourraient parfaitement figurer dans un discours de greenwashing. Mais le premier est une communication du groupe Danone , alors que le second est le titre d’une publication scientifique . Ces ressemblances ne sont pas tellement surprenantes. Nous avons suivi l’émergence et le devenir de 30 nouveaux termes…
